resources.string: Dates are judged by the tithi running at sunrise. Where a tithi spans two sunrises, traditions differ on which day carries the festival.

Judged here by the tithi running at sunrise. It is traditionally timed to midnight, so an almanac following that timing can place it a day either side.
Judged here by the tithi running at sunrise. It is traditionally timed to nishita, the middle of the night, so an almanac following that timing can place it a day either side.
Judged here by the tithi running at sunrise. It is traditionally timed to pradosh, the hour after sunset, so an almanac following that timing can place it a day either side.
The day the Sun entered a new rashi, taken between one sunrise and the next.
Panchanga
Five measures of the day — literally, \"five limbs\".

A panchanga describes a day with five values: the tithi, the vara, the nakshatra, the yoga and the karana. All five come from where the Sun and the Moon actually are, so all five change at their own pace and none of them lines up neatly with the calendar. Reading a day means reading the five together rather than any one alone.
Tithi
The lunar day — how far the Moon has pulled ahead of the Sun.

A tithi is the time the Moon takes to gain another 12° on the Sun, so a lunar month holds thirty of them. The Moon\'s speed varies, so a tithi runs anywhere from about 19 to 26 hours — which is why it starts and ends at a different clock time each day instead of at midnight. A day is named after whichever tithi is running at sunrise.
Paksha
The fortnight — waxing towards full, or waning towards new.

The thirty tithis of a lunar month split into two fortnights of fifteen. Shukla paksha runs from the new moon to the full moon, with the lit part of the Moon growing each night; Krishna paksha runs from full back to new as it shrinks. The same tithi name occurs once in each, so the paksha is what tells them apart.
Vara
The weekday — but counted from sunrise, not from midnight.

The seven varas are the familiar weekdays, each named for a graha. The difference is where the day begins: a vara runs sunrise to sunrise, so the hours after midnight still belong to the previous day. This is also why the windows measured from sunrise — Rahu Kalam among them — shift by a few minutes daily and sit differently in summer than in winter.
Nakshatra
One of 27 equal segments of the Moon\'s path, each 13°20\' wide.

The Moon\'s circuit is divided into twenty-seven nakshatras rather than the twelve rashis, so it crosses roughly one a day. Each carries a traditional name and character. The nakshatra the Moon occupied at birth is the janma nakshatra, which is what most matching and dasha calculations are built from.
Pada
A quarter of a nakshatra — 3°20\' of the Moon\'s path.

Each nakshatra divides into four padas, giving 108 in all. The pada is what connects a nakshatra to a navamsha sign, so it matters for chart work even though it is rarely quoted on its own. The Moon spends roughly six hours in each.
Yoga
A 27-part cycle from the Sun\'s and Moon\'s positions added together.

Yoga is found by adding the Sun\'s and Moon\'s longitudes and dividing the total into twenty-seven parts — it is not a posture or a practice, despite the shared word. Where the tithi measures the gap between the two bodies, the yoga measures how far the pair has travelled as a whole, so it turns over roughly once a day.
Karana
Half a tithi — the quickest of the five limbs.

Each tithi divides into two karanas, so a lunar month holds sixty of them, each lasting about half a day. They are drawn from eleven names: seven that repeat around the month, and four fixed ones that occur once each. It is the fastest limb to change, so it is the one most likely to differ between morning and evening.
Lunar month
Thirty tithis — about 29.5 days, so it drifts against the calendar.

A lunar month runs from one new moon to the next, roughly 29.5 days, which is about a day short of most calendar months. That shortfall is why festivals fixed to a tithi land on a different date each year, and why the lunar and solar years need an extra month (adhika maasa) every few years to stay in step.
The day begins at sunrise
Traditionally the day starts at sunrise, not at midnight.

Almost everything a panchanga measures is counted from sunrise: the day\'s name, the eight equal parts that place Rahu Kalam, the fifteen that place Abhijit. Two consequences catch people out. The hours just after midnight still belong to yesterday\'s vara, and the day\'s tithi can change at any hour — often in the middle of the afternoon.
Moon phase
How much of the Moon is lit — a picture of the tithi.

The phase and the tithi measure the same thing from different ends: both follow the angle between the Sun and the Moon. New moon opens Shukla paksha, full moon closes it, and the shape in the sky is a rough check on the number — a half-lit Moon means the eighth tithi of a fortnight, give or take a few hours.
Rashi
A zodiac sign — one twelfth of the sky, thirty degrees wide.

The twelve rashis divide the ecliptic into equal thirty-degree stretches, measured here against the stars rather than against the equinox, which is what makes them sidereal. The Moon crosses one in about two and a quarter days; the Sun takes roughly a month, and its move into the next one is the sankranti.
Ritu
One of six seasons, each two months of the Sun\'s journey.

The year divides into six ritus of sixty degrees of solar longitude each — Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta and Shishira — so each runs about two months. They are read from where the Sun actually is rather than from a fixed date, which is why a ritu can begin a few days either side of the same day each year. Traditional daily routine is said to shift with them.
Sankalpa
The ten measures that fix when and where a moment is.

A sankalpa traditionally opens by naming the place and then the time — the year, the ayana, the season, the month, the fortnight, the tithi, the weekday, the nakshatra, the yoga and the karana, in that order. Those ten are the same values a panchanga reports, which is much of why it reports them. The order varies by region and tradition.
The roughly 48 minutes before sunrise — traditionally the most auspicious time for meditation, japa, and study, when the mind is calm and sattvic.
A short \'victory\' window around solar noon, auspicious for beginning important tasks; it is said to remove obstacles (but is skipped on Wednesdays).
An inauspicious period of about 90 minutes ruled by Rahu, traditionally avoided for starting new or important undertakings.
An inauspicious daytime period associated with Yama; new ventures and travel are traditionally avoided during it.
A period ruled by Gulika (Mandi), a son of Saturn. It is avoided for auspicious beginnings, though acts started in it are said to recur.
A short inauspicious segment of the day; important or auspicious activities are traditionally postponed until it passes.
A \'to-be-avoided\' window tied to the current nakshatra; new or auspicious activities are traditionally deferred until it ends.
The eleventh lunar day of each fortnight, sacred to Vishnu. Many keep a fast (vrat) for health, discipline, and spiritual merit.
The full-moon day, considered auspicious for worship, charity, and vrats; several major festivals fall on a Purnima.
The new-moon day, traditionally set aside for honouring ancestors (tarpana) and for quiet reflection.
The fourth lunar day of the waning fortnight, dedicated to Ganesha. Devotees fast until moonrise to seek the removal of obstacles.
The fourth lunar day of the waxing fortnight, dedicated to Ganesha and observed with worship for wisdom and success.
The twilight window of the thirteenth lunar day, sacred to Shiva; worship at dusk is held to be especially fruitful.
The monthly night of Shiva, on the fourteenth day of the waning fortnight, observed with worship and a night vigil.
The lunar new year of the Deccan and Maharashtra (Chaitra Shukla Pratipada), welcoming the new samvatsara with festivity and fresh beginnings.
The birth of Lord Rama on Chaitra Shukla Navami, marked by worship, readings of the Ramayana, and processions.
An \'imperishable\' day (Vaishakha Shukla Tritiya) believed to bring lasting merit and prosperity; favoured for new ventures and purchases.
The Vaishakha full moon marking the birth — and by tradition the enlightenment and passing — of Gautama Buddha.
The Ashadha full moon honouring one\'s guru and the sage Vyasa, observed with gratitude and learning.
The Shravana full moon when sisters tie a rakhi on their brothers\' wrists, a symbol of protection and affection.
The birth of Lord Krishna on Shravana Krishna Ashtami, celebrated with fasting, midnight worship, and festivity.
The birthday of Ganesha (Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturthi), welcomed with clay idols and worship, and closed with a ceremonial immersion.
The first of nine nights honouring the Divine Mother (Durga), from Ashwina Shukla Pratipada, with fasting, dance, and worship.
Dussehra — the tenth day celebrating the victory of good over evil (Rama over Ravana, Durga over Mahishasura).
The festival of lights on Kartika Amavasya, honouring Lakshmi with lamps, a cleaned home, and the celebration of prosperity.
The \'great night of Shiva\' in Magha, observed with fasting, a night vigil, and worship of the Shiva linga.
The spring festival of colours on the Phalguna full moon, preceded by Holika Dahan, celebrating joy and the triumph of devotion.
The Sun\'s entry into a new rashi (zodiac sign). Each Sankranti is considered auspicious for bathing in sacred rivers, charity, and worship.
The Sun\'s entry into Makara (Capricorn), marking the start of Uttarayana — its northward journey. Celebrated across India as a harvest festival (Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Lohri).
